Date: 2023-02-24
REMARKS
This Amendment is responsive to the Advisory Action dated June 16, 2022, and the Office Action dated March 28, 2022. Applicant has not amended the previously presented claims, but has presented new claims 32-40. Claims 1-12, 23-27, and 29-40 will be pending upon entry of this Amendment.
Claim Reiection Under 35 U.S.C. 101
The Office Action and Advisory Action rejected claims 1-31 under 35 U.S.C. § 101 based on an assertion that these claims are directed to non-statutory subject matter.
The Subject Matter Eligibility Analysis
To evaluate whether a claim is patentable under 35 U.S.C. § 101, the Office should evaluate the claim under the Subject Matter Eligibility (SME) analysis.1 Under step 1 of the SME analysis, the Office should determine whether the claim is directed to one of the four categories of patentable subject matter - process, machine, manufacture, and composition of matter.2 If the claim is directed to one of the four categories, the SME analysis proceeds to step 2A.3 Under step 2A, the Office should determine whether the claim is directed to a law of nature, a natural phenomenon, or an abstract idea.4 When the claim is not directed to a law of nature, a natural phenomenon, or an abstract idea, the claim is eligible subject matter under 35 U.S.C. § 101. If the Office determines that a claim is directed to a law of nature, a natural phenomenon, or an abstract idea, the SME analysis advances to step 2B.5 Under step 2B, the Office must determine

whether the claim recites additional elements that amount to significantly more than the judicial exception.6 When the claim recites additional elements that amount to significantly more than the judicial exception, the claim is eligible subject matter under 35 U.S.C. § 101, even when the claim is directed to an abstract idea.7 Step 1 of the SME Analysis
The Office has acknowledged that the independent claims 1, 13, and 23 are directed towards "a system and method for identifying premature ventricular contraction (PVC) based on slope intervals and correlation values between a current ventricular depolarization, a preceding adjacent ventricular depolarization, and a subsequent adjacent ventricular depolarization meeting predefined slope or correlation criteria; determining a PVC detection quantification; and communication circuitry that transmits PVC detection quantification data to a user computing device."8 Applicant's new independent claims 32 and 37 are directed towards such systems and techniques. Consequently, the SME analysis proceeds to Step 2A.
Step 2A of the SME Analysis
The Office must apply a two-pronged analysis for determining whether a claim is patentable under step 2A.9 Under prong one, the MPEP states that the Office should "evaluate whether the claim recites a judicial exception."" More specifically, the MPEP advises that abstract ideas fall within at least one of three enumerated groupings - mathematical concepts, certain methods of organizing human activity, and mental processes.1 If the claim recites a judicial exception, the claim requires further analysis under prong two. two, the MPEP states that the Office "should evaluate whether the claim as a whole integrates the recited judicial exception into a practical application of the exception."12 If the claim as a whole integrates the recited judicial exception into a practical application of the exception, the claim is not directed to the judicial exception, and the claim is patentable under 35 U.S.C. § 101.
Prong One Analysis
With respect to prong one of Step 2A, the Office asserted that the previously submitted independent claims recite limitations which fall within the mental processes groupings of abstract ideas.13 More specifically, the Office asserted that the independent claims "covers performance of the method steps in the mind, but for the recitation of generic sensors (i.e. electrodes) and processing and communication circuitry."" Additionally, the Office asserted that "identifying PVC can include a healthcare professional visually identifying ventricular depolarizations, a maximum and minimum slope point, an interval from the maximum slope point to the minimum slope point, and identify PVC if the slope intervals satisfy predetermined slope criteria. Determining a PVC detection quantification can include a healthcare professional quantifying the amount of PVC, and communicating it to the patient or another user."15 Applicant submits that no claim, including claim 1 as representative of all pending claims, falls within the mental processes grouping. The Federal Circuit found that the written description of the '207 patent confirmed that claim 1 of the '207 patent "achieves multiple technological improvements," including that it "more accurately detects the occurrence of atrial fibrillation and atrial flutter ... and allows for more reliable and immediate treatment of these two medical conditions" and "avoids false positives and false negatives," and thus "is able to identify sustained episodes of atrial fibrillation and atrial flutter that have 'increased clinical significance."'24 In reversing the district court's ineligibility finding, the Federal Circuit focused on the district court's "incorrect assumption that the claims are directed to automating known techniques," including because "the written description does not disclose that doctors performed the same techniques as the claimed device in diagnosing atrial fibrillation or atrial flutter."25 Instead, "nothing in the record support[ed] the ... finding . . . that doctors long used the claimed diagnostic processes."26 The Federal Circuit stated that "it is difficult to fathom how doctors mentally or manually" practiced the specific 22 CardioNet, LLC v. Like claim 1 of the '207 patent, claim 1 of the present application relates to a system and technique for monitoring physiological activity and improvements for such devices that doctors had not previously used. Specifically, it discloses a medical system that determines PVCs by "identify[ing] a plurality of ventricular depolarizations within a cardiac electrogram" ("EGM");
"identify[ing] a maximum slope point, a minimum slope point, and an interval from the maximum slope point to the minimum slope point"; and "determin[ing] that the intervals from the maximum slope point to the minimum slope point for the current ventricular depolarization, a preceding adjacent ventricular depolarization of the plurality of ventricular depolarizations, and a subsequent adjacent ventricular depolarization of the plurality of ventricular depolarizations satisfy one or more slope criteria."

In some examples, implementation of certain aspects of the described techniques in hardware may improve the computation and power performance of the implementing device, e.g., IMD 10. As examples, processing circuitry may include hardware configured to compute difference sums or other correlation values, maximum and minimum R-wave amplitudes, maximum and minimum slopes, slope intervals, and differential signals for identifying noise characteristics, and include firmware for other functionality described herein.29

Specifically, "at that time, no insertable cardiac monitors were capable of detecting PVCs," and "physicians had expressed to Medtronic that they desired the LINQ II [insertable cardiac monitoring] device to include functionality for detecting PVCs."31 Mr. Sarkar describes how there were "several significant challenges" to developing the claimed invention, including because the system "had to be developed to use as little computing power as possible in order to enable long-term, continuous PVC monitoring."32 As similarly explained in the PVC Manuscript authored by Mr. Sarkar and others, "[t]he main technical challenge in developing detection algorithms for implantable devices, such as an ICM device, is the fact that one must optimize the algorithm not only for performance but also for computation requirements to minimize batter current drain and preserve longevity of the device," which "limited the performance that could be achieved."33 Another primary challenge was developing a detection technique that would work with the "small, dipole electrodes" used in the LINQ II device, which "could result in an 30 Applicant's originally filed specification, para. For example, although cardiac electrogram signals are conventionally used to measure cardiac activity, a cardiac electrogram signal includes rapid and complex slope changes. It is not feasible for a human to visually identify, with sufficient accuracy for medical purposes, maximum and minimum slope points in the cardiac electrogram signal. Nor is it feasible for a human to calculate, in the mind or with pencil and paper, the slope of the cardiac electrogram or satisfaction of the slope criteria because cardiac electrograms are not simple mathematical functions that can be trivially differentiated.60 As Applicant described earlier, cardiac electrograms are Fourier series that are far more complicated than the quadratic expressions typically in a Calculus textbook.
Claim l's "processing circuitry" accordingly contains PVC-specific hardware that can carry out particular functions like "identify a maximum slope point, a minimum slope point, and an interval from the maximum slope point to the minimum slope point," "determine that the intervals from the maximum slope point to the minimum slope point for the current ventricular depolarization, a preceding adjacent ventricular depolarization of the plurality of ventricular depolarizations, and a subsequent adjacent ventricular depolarization of the plurality of ventricular depolarizations satisfy one or more slope criteria," and "determine that the current ventricular depolarization is a premature ventricular contraction (PVC) based on the intervals from the maximum slope point to the minimum slope point satisfying the one or more slope criteria." Alstom S.A., 830 F.3d 1350, 1354 (Fed. Cir. 2016) ("[W]e have treated analyzing information by steps people go through in their minds, or by mathematical algorithms, without more, as essentially mental processes within the abstract-idea category.").
hardware that carries out requisite PVC-specific computations and noise analysis."61 As such, the limitations of claim 1 could not be performed in the mind or with pencil and paper, but instead require this PVC-specific hardware and related techniques and constitute an improvement to PVC detection technology. This is similar to calculating an exact position of a GPS receiver based on satellite signals and analyzing thousands of network packets in order to identify suspicious network activity, examples which the Federal Circuit has held to be unfeasible for a human.62
Further, the invention of the present application is directed toward a specific technological improvement in PVC detection-not merely applying a preexisting technique using conventional computer equipment. Mr. Sarkar's and Dr. Berger's declarations and documents confirm this. Specifically, Mr. Sarkar explains that no PVC-detection technologies existed for an insertable cardiac monitoring device, and physicians had requested such a device.63 Mr. Sarkar and others then spent years developing the claimed diagnostic technique and system that, as a result, would enable continuous, long-term PVC monitoring and detection.64 The PVC Manuscript also explains that "[t]he main technical challenge in developing detection algorithms for implantable devices, such as an ICM device, is the fact that one must optimize the algorithm not only for performance but also for computation requirements to minimize batter current drain and preserve longevity of the device," which "limited the performance that could be achieved."65 This further highlights the claimed invention's technological achievement.

As Dr. Berger similarly explains, the claimed invention and its development "represents an elegant and significant technical advancement in PVC detection technology," as "continuous long-term [PVC] monitoring was not available or feasible" prior to the invention.66 This advancement is particularly relevant because "analyzing beat-to-beat morphologies also allows the PVC detection system to be more resilient to changes in the device's orientation and the patient's positioning, and to noise in an EGM signal, which can greatly affect an EGM and any resulting PVC detection, including with insertable cardiac monitors."67 The claimed invention thus presents a technical solution - the specific claimed technique of analyzing beat-to-beat morphologies - to a technical problem, particularly in the insertable cardiac monitor context.
Thus, claim 1 does not recite an abstract idea falling into any of the enumerated categories of abstract ideas, so claim 1 and the other claims do not recite an abstract idea.
The new independent claims 32 and 37 also explicitly disclose invention-specific hardware limitations such as a "housing configured for subcutaneous implantation within a patient, the housing having a length, a width, and a depth, wherein the length is greater than each of the width and the depth" and "a plurality of electrodes positioned at the outer surface of the housing and configured to continuously sense a cardiac electrogram of the patient while the insertable cardiac monitor is subcutaneously implanted within the patient over a period of time greater than several days." These limitations incorporate the system's technical components of an insertable cardiac monitor for continuous, long-term monitoring, and further confirm that Applicant's newly presented claims do not recite an abstract idea and instead claim a patent- eligible invention.

Prong Two Analysis
Applicant maintains that claim 1 does not recite an abstract idea. However, even if claim 1 recites an abstract idea, which Applicant does not concede, claim 1 as a whole integrates the recited judicial exception into a practical application of the alleged abstract idea such that claim 1 is not, in effect, a patent to the abstract idea itself.
A claim that integrates an abstract idea into a practical application of the abstract idea relies on the abstract idea in a manner that imposes a meaningful limit on the abstract idea.68 The MPEP specifically provides the following:
Because a judicial exception alone is not eligible subject matter, if there are no additional claim elements besides the judicial exception, or if the additional claim elements merely recite another judicial exception, that is insufficient to integrate the judicial exception into a practical application. However, the way in which the additional elements use or interact with the exception may integrate it into a practical application. Accordingly, the additional limitations should not be evaluated in a vacuum, completely separate from the recited judicial exception. Instead, the analysis should take into consideration all the claim limitations and how those limitations interact and impact each other when evaluating whether the exception is integrated into a practical application.69
Claim 1 integrates processing circuitry configured to "identify a maximum slope point, a minimum slope point, and an interval from the maximum slope point to the minimum slope point," and "determine that the intervals from the maximum slope point to the minimum slope point... satisfy one or more slope criteria" into the practical application of detecting PVCs. As explained above, the claimed invention as a whole is directed at a particular combination of processing and communication circuitry and PVC detection steps to practically apply a specific PVC detection technique in a specific technical context. For example, Dr. Berger describes how, 68 MPEP 2106.04(d).
69 MPEP 2106.04(d) III.
in the device context, the claimed PVC detection system can be "more resilient to changes in the device's orientation and the patient's positioning, and to noise in an EGM signal," which "is crucial for any PVC monitoring system," and generally "allows insertable cardiac monitors to be feasible for long-term, continuous PVC monitoring, and ultimately assists related medical diagnosis and treatment. "70
Thus, claim 1 does not seek to monopolize every single technique for detecting PVCs, and represents a practical application of PVC monitoring via a specific technique of detecting and quantifying PVCs. For example, the claimed invention's use of slope points and slope criteria in analyzing morphology, and the claimed specific hardware, imposes a meaningful limit on the alleged abstract idea, rather than merely adopting the abstract and general concept of detecting PVCs. Any alleged abstract idea thus has "been sufficiently integrated into a practical application" and provide "a practical and real-world technological solution" that "satisfies the requirements of § 101."71
As explained above, the specific claimed technique of detecting PVCs by analyzing beat- to-beat morphologies and practicing the other claim limitations was not used before and could not practically be done in the human mind or with a pencil and paper. As the Board found in a comparable case, there is no indication "that the human mind is equipped" to implement the cited technique, and "nothing of record suggests that the claimed [invention] represents an automated implementation of techniques humans would likely use."72 Claim 1 thus is patent-eligible.

Step 2B of the SME Analysis
Applicant submits that claim 1 is not directed to an abstract idea. But even if claim 1 were directed to an abstract idea, it recites additional elements that amount to significantly more than the alleged abstract idea and provide an inventive concept. For example, claim 1 includes limitations that are not well-understood, routine, conventional activity in the field, which is indicative that an inventive concept is present,77 such that claim 1 recites eligible subject matter.
Step 2B of the SME analysis involves "first identifying whether there are any additional elements (features/limitations/steps) recited in the claim beyond the judicial exception(s), and then evaluating those additional elements individually and in combination to determine whether they contribute an inventive concept (i.e., amount to significantly more than the judicial exception(s))."78 In determining whether a claim recites additional elements that amount to significantly more than an abstract idea, the Office should (1) identify any additional elements " See 2019 Revised Eligibility Guidance, at p. 56. 78 MPEP 2106.05 II.
recited in the claim that are beyond the abstract idea, and (2) evaluate those additional elements individually and in combination to determine whether they contribute to an inventive concept.79 Claim 1 of the present application does not recite processing circuitry of a medical device system merely as a tool, but rather as circuitry specifically configured to carry out PVC-specific detection and analysis. Both Mr. Sarkar and Dr. Berger have explained how the claimed invention's detection of PVCs by analyzing beat-to-beat morphologies presented a technological advancement that solved technical problems with previous PVC detection techniques and systems, including Holter monitors and insertable cardiac monitors, and thus enabled long-term PVC monitoring for the first time.80 Mr. Sarkar further describes the claimed invention's "PVC- specific hardware" that "carries out requisite PVC-specific computations and noise analysis" and thus can carry out the limitations of claim 1.81 The invention in claim 1 amounts to significantly more than an alleged abstract idea and represents a patent-eligible inventive concept.
